I would treat this as an urgent **hold-and-review**, not let the payroll run automatically end Ryan’s employment on the basis of this code.

On the internal code definitions alone, his absence is not SC—he says he was not ill—or BRV. His sister lives elsewhere and is not among the relationships listed for DEP, and it cannot be booked as annual leave after the event. So the literal codebook points to UA; telling Gary before the shift does not, by itself, mean the absence was booked in advance.

But there is an important legal issue the codebook may not capture. UK statutory time-off-for-dependants rules can include someone who reasonably relies on the employee for assistance. Ryan’s account—that his sister went into labour unexpectedly, her husband could not return, their mother was far away, and he took his sister to hospital—makes that a credible possibility. I would not let a second-UA termination letter go out before that is reviewed.

At once, I would contact the HR Manager and an authorised senior or payroll contact, explain the facts and the noon deadline, and request that Ryan’s entry and termination letter be held pending review. I would use any available hold or exception process rather than leave the SC code in place as though it were true, or force the facts into a code that may not fit. I would record his account factually in a note, but not treat the note as a substitute for resolving the payroll code: it does not affect payroll or probation. I also would not demand evidence, since the stated process does not require it.
